1235	All dates are `datetime.date`; nothing here looks at the clock.
1236	
1237	### The schedule words
1238	
1239	`parse_schedule(text)` returns a `Schedule` and understands exactly these shapes:
1240	
1241	| text | meaning |
1242	|---|---|
1243	| `daily` | every day |
1244	| `weekly on mon` | every Monday; the day is `mon tue wed thu fri sat sun` |
1245	| `monthly on 5` | the 5th of every month; a number from 1 to 31 |
1246	| `monthly on last` | the last day of every month |
1247	| `yearly on 03-15` | every 15 March; `MM-DD`, two digits each |
1248	| `every 2 weeks from 2024-01-03` | the given date, then every 2 weeks after it |
1249	| `every 3 months from 2024-01-31` | the given date, then every 3 months after it |
1250	
1251	The `every` form is `every N UNIT from DATE`: `N` is a whole number of at least 1, `UNIT` is `days`, `weeks`,
1252	`months` or `years` (or the singular `day`, `week`, `month`, `year`, with any `N`), and `DATE` is a real
1253	`YYYY-MM-DD` date.
1254	
1255	Capitals and the amount of blank space between the words or around the text do not matter (`Monthly On LAST` is
1256	fine). Anything that is not one of these shapes (`daily on mon`, `weekly`, `monthly on 0`, `monthly on 32`,
1257	`weekly on someday`, `yearly on 13-01`, `yearly on 02-30`, `yearly on 3-15`, `every 0 days from 2024-01-01`,
1258	`every 2 weeks`, `every 2 fortnights from 2024-01-01`, `every 2 weeks from 2024-02-30`, an empty text, a value
1259	that is not text) raises `RecurringError`, a `tallybook.errors.ValidationError` (code `validation`), whose message
1260	names the shapes that are allowed.
1261	
1262	A `Schedule` is an immutable, hashable value; schedules that mean the same are equal (`Daily` and `daily`, or
1263	`every 1 week from 2024-01-03` and `every 1 weeks from 2024-01-03`). `str(schedule)` is the canonical text: lower
1264	case, single spaces, `monthly on last`, `yearly on 03-15` with two digits, and in the `every` form the unit
1265	singular when `N` is 1 and plural otherwise (`every 1 week from 2024-01-03`, `every 2 weeks from 2024-01-03`).
1266	Parsing the canonical text gives back an equal schedule.
1267	
1268	`schedule.between(start, end)` is the list of the schedule's own dates from `start` to `end`, both included,
1269	ascending (a Schedule knows nothing about a series' start, end or count).
1270	
1271	### Which dates a schedule produces
1272	
1273	- `daily`: every day. `weekly on mon`: every date that is a Monday.
1274	- `monthly on N`: the Nth day of every month; a month too short for it gets its last day, so `monthly on 31` gives
1275	  31 Jan, 29 Feb 2024, 31 Mar, 30 Apr and `monthly on 30` gives 28 Feb 2023. `monthly on last` is the last day
1276	  whatever the length.
1277	- `yearly on MM-DD`: that day every year; `yearly on 02-29` gives 29 Feb in leap years and 28 Feb in the others.
1278	- `every N days from D` and `every N weeks from D` (a week is 7 days): D, D plus N days (or weeks), plus twice
1279	  that, and so on; nothing before D. `every 10 days from 2024-01-01` gives 1, 11, 21, 31 January, 10 February.
1280	- `every N months from D` and `every N years from D` (a year is 12 months): the k-th date is D moved forward by
1281	  k times N months, counted from D itself and not from the previous date, the day clamped to the end of the month
1282	  when needed; nothing before D. So `every 1 months from 2024-01-31` gives 01-31, 02-29, 03-31, 04-30, 05-31 (no
1283	  drift to the 30th), `every 3 months from 2024-01-31` gives 2024-01-31, 04-30, 07-31, 10-31, 2025-01-31, and
1284	  `every 1 years from 2024-02-29` gives 2024-02-29, then 28 Feb 2025, 2026 and 2027, then 2028-02-29.
1285	
1286	### A recurring item
1287	
1288	`Recurring(name, schedule, template, start, end=None, count=None)`:
1289	
1290	- `name`: text of ASCII letters, digits, `-` and `_`, not beginning with `-` or `_` (`rent`, `phone-bill`, `2024_tax`).
1291	- `schedule`: a `Schedule`, or text, which is parsed with `parse_schedule` (so a bad text raises
1292	  `RecurringError`). The attribute `.schedule` is always a `Schedule`.
1293	- `template`: a `tallybook.model.Transaction`. Its own date means nothing; its payee, narration, flag, tags and
1294	  postings are what the copies are made from.
1295	- `start`: the first day the series may produce a date. `end`: the last day, included, or `None`. `count`: the
1296	  most dates the series ever produces, or `None`; it counts the dates produced from `start` on, so it never
1297	  depends on which stretch of time is asked about later.
1298	
1299	The attributes `.name .schedule .template .start .end .count` are readable. Items with equal attributes are equal.
1300	Anything wrong (a name that does not fit, a schedule that is not a `Schedule` or text, a template that is not a
1301	`Transaction`, a `start` that is not a date, an `end` that is not a date or is before `start`, a `count` that is
1302	not an `int` of at least 1, `True` included) is a `RecurringError`.
1303	
1304	`occurrences(rec, start, end)` returns the dates of the series within the window `start` to `end`, both
1305	included, ascending, as a list (an `end` before `start` gives `[]`). The series is the schedule's dates that are
1306	on or after `rec.start`, up to and including `rec.end` if there is one, and no more than `rec.count` of them,
1307	counted from the first. Some consequences:
1308	
1309	- A start on a day the schedule hits includes that day (`weekly on mon` from Monday 2024-01-01 gives 2024-01-01
1310	  first); `monthly on 5` starting 2024-02-10 gives 2024-03-05 first.
1311	- With `count=3`, a January start and `monthly on 5`, the dates are 5 Jan, 5 Feb, 5 Mar, even when I ask only
1312	  about April to June (nothing comes back then).
1313	- `end` and `count` both apply; whichever stops the series first wins.
1314	- The `every` forms keep the rhythm of the date after `from` even if the item starts later: `every 2 weeks from
1315	  2024-01-03` with `start=2024-01-20` gives 2024-01-31, 2024-02-14, 2024-02-28... (and never anything before
1316	  2024-01-03, even when `start` is earlier).
1317	
1318	### Copies of the template
1319	
1320	`expand(recs, start, end)` returns a list of new `Transaction` objects, one for every date of every item in the
1321	window, ordered by date, then item name (plain text order), then the item's position in `recs`. A copy has:
1322	
1323	- `date` the occurrence date; `payee`, `narration` and `flag` equal to the template's; `id` `None`;
1324	- `postings`: a new list holding the template's postings in order (a posting without an amount stays without one);
1325	- `tags`: a tuple of the template's tags plus the tag `recurring`, each once, sorted.
1326	
1327	The template is never changed, and changing a copy's list of postings changes neither the template nor the other
1328	copies. `instantiate(rec, on)` builds the single copy dated `on` the same way (it does not check that `on` is one
1329	of the item's dates).

1331	For example, with a template tagged `home`, `expand([rent], date(2024, 2, 1), date(2024, 3, 31))` for the item

1374	### Conventions all reports share
1375	
1376	- A report `dict` contains only dicts, lists, strings, booleans, `None` and integers. Its key `"report"` is
1377	  `"trial_balance"`, `"balance_sheet"`, `"income_statement"`, `"cashflow"`, `"register"` or `"net_worth"`.
1378	- Money is always `{"amount": "12.50", "currency": "USD"}` (amount text with the currency's own number of
1379	  decimals, a leading `-` when negative, no thousands separators). Dates are `"YYYY-MM-DD"` text.
1380	- The type of an account comes from its first path segment: `Assets` asset, `Liabilities` liability, `Equity`
1381	  equity, `Income` income, `Expenses` expense.
1382	- Lists of accounts are sorted by account path as plain text, character by character (`Expenses:Food-X` comes
1383	  before `Expenses:Food:Alpha` because `-` sorts before `:`), then by currency code; lists of money per currency by
1384	  currency code. Postings are never rolled up into parent accounts unless stated.
1385	- A zero balance is left out of an account list. (Lists of money per currency are described report by report.)
1386	- Dates mean whole days, both ends of a `Period` included. A "balance on D" counts every posting dated on or
1387	  before D.
1388	- Percentages are text with exactly one decimal (`"5.7"`, `"100.0"`, `"-2.5"`), rounded to the nearest tenth of a
1389	  percent, an exact half going away from zero (0.25 becomes `0.3`); a zero result is `"0.0"`, never `"-0.0"`.
1390	- Converting to one currency (`convert_to="EUR"`) uses the exchange rates the ledger knows: its attribute `rates`,
1391	  the `RateTable` it was created with (an empty table if none), at the rate in force on the date given below, one
1392	  amount at a time, as the currency module converts money. A missing rate raises the currency module's own
1393	  `CurrencyError` as it is, and so does a `convert_to` that is not a known currency.

1407	| 6 | 2024-03-12 | Corner | Expenses:Food +12.00, Assets:Cash -12.00 |
1408	| 7 | 2024-04-02 | Card payoff | Liabilities:Card +900.00, Checking -900.00 |
1409	| 8 | 2024-04-03 | Market | Expenses:Food +30.00, Checking -30.00 |
1410	
1411	### trial_balance(ledger, as_of)
1412	
1413	`as_of` is a date, or `None` for every posting. The result:
1414	
1415	```
1416	{"report": "trial_balance", "as_of": "2024-03-31",
1417	 "accounts": [{"account": "Assets:Cash", "type": "asset", "debit": {money}, "credit": null}, ...],
1418	 "totals": [{"currency": "USD", "debit": {money}, "credit": {money}, "balanced": true}]}
1419	```
1420	
1421	`as_of` is `null` when `None` was given. `accounts` has one entry per account and currency whose balance is not
1422	zero: a positive balance is in `debit` (`credit` is `null`), a negative one as its absolute value in `credit`
1423	(`debit` is `null`). `totals` has one entry per currency appearing in `accounts`: the sum of the debits, the sum of
1424	the credits, and `balanced`, true when the two are equal. For the sample book on 2024-03-31 the single total is
1425	4400.00 and 4400.00. An empty ledger gives empty lists.
1426	
1427	### balance_sheet(ledger, as_of, convert_to=None, today=None)
1428	
1429	```
1430	{"report": "balance_sheet", "as_of": "2024-03-31", "currency": null,
1431	 "assets":      {"accounts": [{"account": "Assets:Cash", "balance": {money}}, ...], "total": [{money}, ...]},
1432	 "liabilities": {"accounts": [...], "total": [...]},
1433	 "equity":      {"accounts": [...], "retained_earnings": [{money}, ...], "total": [...]},
1434	 "balanced": true}
1435	```
1436	
1437	- `as_of` is a date or `None` (everything); `currency` is `convert_to` or `null`.
1438	- Assets, liabilities and equity each list the accounts of that type with a non-zero balance, one entry per
1439	  account and currency. An asset balance is the sum of its postings; a liability or equity balance has its sign
1440	  turned round, so money owed is positive.
1441	- `retained_earnings` is income less expenses of every posting up to `as_of`, per currency, as a list of money
1442	  sorted by currency without zero results. It is part of `equity.total`, which makes the sheet balance.
1443	- `total` of a section is a list with the sum of the section's lines for each currency that has a line (for
1444	  equity also the retained earnings), sorted by currency; `[]` when the section has nothing.
1445	- `balanced` is true when for every currency `assets.total` equals `liabilities.total` plus `equity.total`
1446	  (a missing currency counts as zero).
1447	- With `convert_to`: every account line is converted separately at the rate on `as_of` (a line already in
1448	  `convert_to` is left as it is) and becomes `{"account", "balance": converted money, "original": the money
1449	  before converting}`; each retained-earnings amount is converted separately and they are added into a single
1450	  entry (a list of one) when any was non-zero; every `total` is then a list of exactly one money in `convert_to`,
1451	  zero if the section is empty. `balanced` is computed on the converted figures. Converting needs a date:
1452	  `convert_to` with `as_of=None` is a `ReportError`.
1453	- `today` is accepted for the day the command line and the web interface will pass, and has no effect.

1459	 "income":   {"accounts": [{"account": "Income:Salary", "amount": {money}, "percent": "100.0"}], "total": [{money}]},
1460	 "expenses": {"accounts": [...same line shape...], "total": [{money}]},
1461	 "net": [{money}]}

1465	round (earning 2500.00 is `2500.00`), an expense is as it is. Each section lists one line per account and
1466	currency with a non-zero amount; `percent` is the line's share of the section total in the same currency (`"0.0"`
1467	when that total is zero; a negative line, a refund, gives a negative percentage). `total` is the list of section
1468	sums per currency that have a line, `[]` when there is none. `net` has, for every currency in either total, income
1469	less expenses, sorted by currency (zero included).
1470	
1471	With `convert_to` each line is converted separately at the rate on the last day of the period and gets an
1472	`"original"` key holding the money before converting; the totals and `net` are then single-entry lists in
1473	`convert_to` (zero if empty), and the percentages are shares of the converted totals.

1476	
1477	Cash means all asset accounts together; what went in and out is told by the account on the other side of each
1478	transaction. For every transaction dated in the period, work per currency: sum its postings to asset accounts;
1479	when that sum is not zero, every posting of the same currency to a non-asset account moves the opposite of its own
1480	amount into the category that account names (a salary posting of -2500.00 puts +2500.00 in, an expense posting of
1481	+54.50 puts -54.50, a card payoff posting of +900.00 on `Liabilities:Card` puts -900.00). A transaction that only
1482	moves money between asset accounts (sum zero) contributes nothing. Then, per account and currency, the
1483	contributions of the period are added: a positive result is an inflow, a negative one an outflow (shown as a
1484	positive amount), zero is left out.

1488	 "opening": [{money}], "inflows": [{"account": "Income:Salary", "amount": {money}}],
1489	 "outflows": [{"account": ..., "amount": {money}}], "total_in": [{money}], "total_out": [{money}],
1490	 "net": [{money}], "closing": [{money}]}
1491	```
1492	
1493	`opening` is the asset balance before the period starts, `closing` the one after its last day, `net` the change
1494	(`total_in - total_out`, equal to `closing - opening`). The money lists (`opening`, `total_in`, `total_out`, `net`,
1495	`closing`) have one entry for every currency of any asset posting dated on or before the end of the period (zero
1496	included), sorted by currency; `inflows` and `outflows` are sorted by account then currency. In the sample, March has
1497	opening 1000.00, inflow Salary 2500.00, outflow Food 54.50 (the transfer to Cash cancels, Cash spending counts),
1498	closing 3445.50; April has opening 3445.50, no inflow, outflows Food 30.00 and `Liabilities:Card` 900.00, closing
1499	2515.50.

## The book file: `tallybook.storage`

The whole book lives in one SQLite file (Python's `sqlite3`) that I can copy, back up and mail to my accountant. A class `Store` sits under the command line and the web API, and I use it from scripts: `from tallybook.storage import Store, LATEST_VERSION`; `LATEST_VERSION` is `4`. Old books of mine (made by earlier versions, and by hand) must keep working, so this section says exactly what the file looks like; I will build such files with `sqlite3` and open them with your code.

### Opening and creating

`Store.open(path, create=False)` returns a `Store`; `path` is text or a path object.

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| file missing, `create=False` | `NotFoundError` |
| file missing, `create=True` | created and brought to `LATEST_VERSION`; a missing parent directory is a `NotFoundError` |
| file exists, `create=True` | opened as is: nothing erased, nothing migrated (but see the empty file below) |
| not a SQLite file (a text file, say), or a directory | `ConflictError` |
| a SQLite file with tables but no version marker (somebody else's database) | `ConflictError` |
| a book whose version is higher than `LATEST_VERSION` | `ConflictError`, nothing touched |
| an empty SQLite file (zero bytes) | opens at version 0; with `create=True` it is migrated to the latest version |

A `Store` is a context manager (leaving the block closes it) and has `close()`; afterwards every operation raises `ConflictError`. Several `Store` objects may read the same file at once; a writer waits up to five seconds for another writer, then fails with `ConflictError`.

### The version and the migrations

The schema version is SQLite's `PRAGMA user_version`; `store.version` reports it. Opening an older book does **not** change it: `store.version` is smaller than `LATEST_VERSION`, and every operation except `version`, `migrate()` and `close()` raises `ConflictError` with the message ``database is at version 2, run `tallybook db migrate` `` (the real number). `store.migrate()` applies the missing steps in order and returns the versions it applied (`[3, 4]`; `[]` when current). Each step runs in its own transaction together with its version bump, so a failing step leaves the file exactly at the version before it (earlier steps stay applied) and `migrate()` raises `ConflictError` with a message starting `migration to version N failed:`. There are no down-migrations and no other bookkeeping table.

Dates are stored as `YYYY-MM-DD` text, money as an integer count of minor units plus a currency code. Table and column names are exact.

**Version 1** (the first release)

```sql
CREATE TABLE accounts (path TEXT PRIMARY KEY, type TEXT NOT NULL, currency TEXT, opened TEXT,
                       note TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '');
CREATE TABLE transactions (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, date TEXT NOT NULL, payee TEXT NOT NULL,
                           narration TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '', cleared INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1);
CREATE TABLE postings (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
                       tx_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES transactions(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
                       seq INTEGER NOT NULL, account TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(path),
                       minor INTEGER NOT NULL, currency TEXT NOT NULL);
```

(plus indexes on `transactions(date, id)` and `postings(tx_id, seq)`, which a hand-built file may lack). `accounts.currency` was free text: lower-case, padded with blanks, or empty. `cleared` is 1 (cleared) or 0 (pending). The postings of a transaction are numbered by `seq` from 0.

**Version 2** adds `tags`, `transactions.flag` and `postings.note`:

```sql
CREATE TABLE tags (tx_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES transactions(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, tag TEXT NOT NULL,
                   PRIMARY KEY (tx_id, tag));
ALTER TABLE transactions ADD COLUMN flag TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '*';
ALTER TABLE postings ADD COLUMN note TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '';
```

The step turns `cleared` into the flag: 1 becomes `'*'`, 0 becomes `'!'`; a `cleared` that is not 0 or 1 (or is NULL) makes the step fail and change nothing. The `cleared` column stays; from version 2 on the store keeps it `1` for flag `*` and `0` for `!`, but never reads it. Existing postings get the empty note; no existing transaction gets tags.

**Version 3** adds `rates` and `accounts.closed`:

```sql
CREATE TABLE rates (src TEXT NOT NULL, dst TEXT NOT NULL, on_date TEXT NOT NULL, rate_text TEXT NOT NULL,
                    PRIMARY KEY (src, dst, on_date));
ALTER TABLE accounts ADD COLUMN closed TEXT;
```

The step cleans `accounts.currency` and `postings.currency`: trim blanks, upper-case. An account currency empty after trimming becomes NULL. Anything else that is not exactly three letters after cleaning (`dollars`) makes the step fail and change nothing; so does an empty posting currency. Existing accounts get `closed` NULL.

**Version 4** adds five empty tables and touches no existing row:

```sql
CREATE TABLE budgets (pattern TEXT NOT NULL, period_kind TEXT NOT NULL, minor INTEGER NOT NULL,
                      currency TEXT NOT NULL, start_date TEXT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (pattern, period_kind));
CREATE TABLE recurring (name TEXT PRIMARY KEY, schedule TEXT NOT NULL, template TEXT NOT NULL,
                        start_date TEXT NOT NULL, end_date TEXT, max_count INTEGER, materialized_through TEXT);
CREATE TABLE rules (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY CHECK (id = 1), body TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE settings (key TEXT PRIMARY KEY, value TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE import_keys (key TEXT PRIMARY KEY, tx_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES transactions(id) ON DELETE CASCADE);
```

A step that cannot create its tables (one of that name already exists, say) fails and changes nothing. A book created from nothing goes through all four steps, so it ends up exactly like a migrated one. Foreign keys are enforced, but deleting a transaction must also remove its postings, tags and import key in a book whose old tables lack the cascades.

### Accounts

Accounts are validated by `Chart.add`, so the same errors arise (invalid path, wrong type, unknown currency, existing path).

- `add_account(path, type=None, currency=None, opened=None, note="") -> Account` stores it and returns the stored `Account`; `get_account(path) -> Account` (`NotFoundError`).
- `accounts(type=None, under=None, currency=None, include_closed=True) -> list[Account]` sorted by path. `type` is `asset`, `liability`, `equity`, `income` or `expense` (else `ValidationError`); `under` keeps that account and everything below it; `currency` keeps accounts of that currency; `include_closed=False` drops closed ones. Only accounts that were added are listed, not parents that merely exist as part of a longer path.
- `count_accounts(...)`: the same filters, returns a number.
- `chart() -> Chart`: a fresh in-memory chart of the stored accounts, closed ones closed.
- `close_account(path, on) -> Account` closes the account as of `on` (usable that day). `NotFoundError` for an unknown account; closing twice or before the opening date is the chart's error; closing earlier than a posting already in the account is a `ConflictError`.
- `set_account_note(path, note) -> Account`; `delete_account(path)` removes an account nothing has posted to (`ConflictError` otherwise, `NotFoundError` if unknown).

### Transactions

- `add_transaction(tx) -> Transaction` (the shared record) validates through a `Ledger` over the stored chart and rates, so the ledger's rules and `LedgerError` apply. Nothing is stored on failure. The result has its `id`, filled-in amounts, and tags sorted without duplicates. An `id` on the input is ignored. Ids are 1, 2, 3 ... and never handed out again, even after the highest was deleted.
- `transactions(query=None, limit=None, offset=0) -> list` in order of `(date, id)`. `query` is query text or a parsed `Query` (an `account:` pattern in query text that matches no account of the book is a `QueryError`); blank or `None` means everything. The filter comes first, then `offset` are skipped, then at most `limit` are returned. `limit` and `offset` are whole numbers of at least 0, else `ValidationError`; only `limit` may be `None` (unlimited).
- `count_transactions(query=None) -> int` counts what `transactions(query)` returns without paging; `has_import_key(key) -> bool`.
- `get_transaction(id)` (`NotFoundError`); `delete_transaction(id) -> Transaction` removes it with its postings, tags and import key and returns what was removed (`NotFoundError` if absent).
- `ledger() -> Ledger`: an in-memory ledger of the whole book (stored ids kept); changing it does not change the book.
- `add_transactions(txs, keys=None) -> BulkAdd` adds many, all or nothing; the result has `.added` (the stored transactions) and `.skipped` (the input positions skipped). `keys` is one text per transaction (else `ValidationError`); a transaction whose key is already an import key, or was recorded earlier in the same call, is skipped; the key of each added one is recorded. If any transaction is invalid nothing at all is added, and the error (otherwise the ledger's own) has a `.detail` dictionary with `"index"`, the position of the bad one.

### Rates, budgets, recurring items

## The book file: `tallybook.storage`

The whole book lives in one SQLite file (Python's `sqlite3`) that I can copy, back up and mail to my accountant. A class `Store` sits under the command line and the web API, and I use it from scripts: `from tallybook.storage import Store, LATEST_VERSION`; `LATEST_VERSION` is `4`. Old books of mine (made by earlier versions, and by hand) must keep working, so this section says exactly what the file looks like; I will build such files with `sqlite3` and open them with your code.

### Opening and creating

`Store.open(path, create=False)` returns a `Store`; `path` is text or a path object.

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| file missing, `create=False` | `NotFoundError` |
| file missing, `create=True` | created and brought to `LATEST_VERSION`; a missing parent directory is a `NotFoundError` |
| file exists, `create=True` | opened as is: nothing erased, nothing migrated (but see the empty file below) |
| not a SQLite file (a text file, say), or a directory | `ConflictError` |
| a SQLite file with tables but no version marker (somebody else's database) | `ConflictError` |
| a book whose version is higher than `LATEST_VERSION` | `ConflictError`, nothing touched |
| an empty SQLite file (zero bytes) | opens at version 0; with `create=True` it is migrated to the latest version |

A `Store` is a context manager (leaving the block closes it) and has `close()`; afterwards every operation raises `ConflictError`. Several `Store` objects may read the same file at once; a writer waits up to five seconds for another writer, then fails with `ConflictError`.

### The version and the migrations

The schema version is SQLite's `PRAGMA user_version`; `store.version` reports it. Opening an older book does **not** change it: `store.version` is smaller than `LATEST_VERSION`, and every operation except `version`, `migrate()` and `close()` raises `ConflictError` with the message ``database is at version 2, run `tallybook db migrate` `` (the real number). `store.migrate()` applies the missing steps in order and returns the versions it applied (`[3, 4]`; `[]` when current). Each step runs in its own transaction together with its version bump, so a failing step leaves the file exactly at the version before it (earlier steps stay applied) and `migrate()` raises `ConflictError` with a message starting `migration to version N failed:`. There are no down-migrations and no other bookkeeping table.

Dates are stored as `YYYY-MM-DD` text, money as an integer count of minor units plus a currency code. Table and column names are exact.

**Version 1** (the first release)

```sql
CREATE TABLE accounts (path TEXT PRIMARY KEY, type TEXT NOT NULL, currency TEXT, opened TEXT,
                       note TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '');
CREATE TABLE transactions (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, date TEXT NOT NULL, payee TEXT NOT NULL,
                           narration TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '', cleared INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1);
CREATE TABLE postings (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
                       tx_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES transactions(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
                       seq INTEGER NOT NULL, account TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(path),
                       minor INTEGER NOT NULL, currency TEXT NOT NULL);
```

(plus indexes on `transactions(date, id)` and `postings(tx_id, seq)`, which a hand-built file may lack). `accounts.currency` was free text: lower-case, padded with blanks, or empty. `cleared` is 1 (cleared) or 0 (pending). The postings of a transaction are numbered by `seq` from 0.

**Version 2** adds `tags`, `transactions.flag` and `postings.note`:

```sql
CREATE TABLE tags (tx_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES transactions(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, tag TEXT NOT NULL,
                   PRIMARY KEY (tx_id, tag));
ALTER TABLE transactions ADD COLUMN flag TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '*';
ALTER TABLE postings ADD COLUMN note TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '';
```

The step turns `cleared` into the flag: 1 becomes `'*'`, 0 becomes `'!'`; a `cleared` that is not 0 or 1 (or is NULL) makes the step fail and change nothing. The `cleared` column stays; from version 2 on the store keeps it `1` for flag `*` and `0` for `!`, but never reads it. Existing postings get the empty note; no existing transaction gets tags.

**Version 3** adds `rates` and `accounts.closed`:

```sql
CREATE TABLE rates (src TEXT NOT NULL, dst TEXT NOT NULL, on_date TEXT NOT NULL, rate_text TEXT NOT NULL,
                    PRIMARY KEY (src, dst, on_date));
ALTER TABLE accounts ADD COLUMN closed TEXT;
```

The step cleans `accounts.currency` and `postings.currency`: trim blanks, upper-case. An account currency empty after trimming becomes NULL. Anything else that is not exactly three letters after cleaning (`dollars`) makes the step fail and change nothing; so does an empty posting currency. Existing accounts get `closed` NULL.

**Version 4** adds five empty tables and touches no existing row:

```sql
CREATE TABLE budgets (pattern TEXT NOT NULL, period_kind TEXT NOT NULL, minor INTEGER NOT NULL,
                      currency TEXT NOT NULL, start_date TEXT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (pattern, period_kind));
CREATE TABLE recurring (name TEXT PRIMARY KEY, schedule TEXT NOT NULL, template TEXT NOT NULL,
                        start_date TEXT NOT NULL, end_date TEXT, max_count INTEGER, materialized_through TEXT);
CREATE TABLE rules (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY CHECK (id = 1), body TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE settings (key TEXT PRIMARY KEY, value TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE import_keys (key TEXT PRIMARY KEY, tx_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES transactions(id) ON DELETE CASCADE);
```

A step that cannot create its tables (one of that name already exists, say) fails and changes nothing. A book created from nothing goes through all four steps, so it ends up exactly like a migrated one. Foreign keys are enforced, but deleting a transaction must also remove its postings, tags and import key in a book whose old tables lack the cascades.

### Accounts

Accounts are validated by `Chart.add`, so the same errors arise (invalid path, wrong type, unknown currency, existing path).

- `accounts(type=None, under=None, currency=None, include_closed=True) -> list[Account]` sorted by path. `type` is `asset`, `liability`, `equity`, `income` or `expense` (else `ValidationError`); `under` keeps that account and everything below it; `currency` keeps accounts of that currency; `include_closed=False` drops closed ones. - `count_accounts(...)`: the same filters, returns a number.
- `chart() -> Chart`: a fresh in-memory chart of the stored accounts, closed ones closed.
- `close_account(path, on) -> Account` closes the account as of `on` (usable that day). `NotFoundError` for an unknown account; closing twice or before the opening date is the chart's error; closing earlier than a posting already in the account is a `ConflictError`.

### Exchange rates

A `RateTable` remembers what one currency was worth in another on particular days. A new table is empty.

```python
rates = RateTable()
rates.set("USD", "EUR", "0.9215", date(2024, 3, 1))
rates.rate("USD", "EUR", date(2024, 3, 15))   # Fraction(1843, 2000)
```

**`set(src, dst, rate_text, on)`** records that **one unit of `src` buys `rate_text` units of `dst`** from day `on` (a
`datetime.date`) onward. It returns nothing.

- `src` and `dst` must be currencies in the table and must differ; otherwise `CurrencyError`.
- `rate_text` must be **text** holding a positive decimal: digits, optionally a `.` followed by 1 to 8 digits. So
  `"150.5"`, `"0.9215"`, `"1"`, `"007.5"` and `"0.00000001"` are fine. Refused with `CurrencyError` (message containing
  the text): `"0"`, `"0.0"`, `"-1.5"`, `"+1.5"`, `".5"`, `"1."`, `"1,5"`, `"1e-3"`, `"1/2"`, `""`, `"abc"`, text with
  spaces or other kinds of digit characters, and anything with more than 8 decimals (`"1.123456789"`, even if the
  extra digits are zeros). Anything that is not text (a float, an int, a `Fraction`,
  `None`) is refused too: `0.9` and `2` are errors.
- `on` must be a `datetime.date`; a string like `"2024-03-01"`, `None` or a number is a `CurrencyError`, and so it is
  for `rate`, `convert` and `remove`. Every function here refuses an unknown or non-string currency code with
  `CurrencyError`.
- The rate is kept **exactly**, as a `fractions.Fraction`, never a float.
- Setting a rate for the same `(src, dst, on)` again **replaces** the earlier one.
- A rate is stored for one direction only; the opposite direction is worked out when asked.

A refused `set` changes nothing.

**`rate(src, dst, on)`** returns the rate in force on day `on` as a `Fraction`:

1. If `src == dst` it is `Fraction(1)` (both codes still have to be known currencies).
2. Otherwise, the rate set for `src -> dst` with the **latest date on or before `on`**. A rate dated the same day
   counts; a later one does not.
3. If no `src -> dst` rate is dated on or before `on`, the **inverse** of the rate set for `dst -> src` with the latest
   date on or before `on`, i.e. `1 / that_rate`, exactly.
4. Otherwise `CurrencyError` with the message `no rate USD -> EUR on 2024-03-01` (the codes and date asked for).

Two points I care about. A **direct rate always beats an inverse one**: as soon as any direct `src -> dst` rate is
dated on or before the day, it is used, even if an opposite-direction rate is more recent. And tallybook **never goes
through a third currency**: with `USD -> EUR` and `EUR -> GBP` set, `USD -> GBP` is an error. I would rather be told
than get a made-up rate.

After `set("USD", "EUR", "0.5", 2024-03-01)` and `set("USD", "EUR", "0.75", 2024-03-10)`:

| asked | answer |
|---|---|
| `rate("USD","EUR", 2024-02-29)` | error: no rate USD -> EUR on 2024-02-29 |
| `rate("USD","EUR", 2024-03-01)` | `Fraction(1, 2)` |
| `rate("USD","EUR", 2024-03-10)` | `Fraction(3, 4)` |
| `rate("EUR","USD", 2024-03-10)` | `Fraction(4, 3)` (the inverse of 3/4) |
| `rate("GBP","GBP", anything)` | `Fraction(1)` |

If `EUR -> USD` is also set to `"1.5"` on 2024-03-02, then `rate("EUR","USD", 2024-03-10)` is `3/2` (the direct rate
beats the inverse of `USD -> EUR`), while `rate("USD","EUR", ...)` still reads the `USD -> EUR` entries.

**`convert(money, dst, on)`** returns a `Money` in currency `dst`: the amount converted at `rate(money.currency, dst,
on)`. It converts the **value**, allowing for the different numbers of decimals, and rounds to a whole minor unit of
`dst` with `round_div` (see Money). With `e_src` and `e_dst` the two exponents, the new minor units are the old
minor units times the rate times `10 ** (e_dst - e_src)`, rounded.

- Converting to the same currency returns the same amount (no rate needed; `dst` must still be a known currency).
- `100.00 USD` to JPY at `150.5` is `15050 JPY` (10000 minor units × 150.5 ÷ 100). `1.00 USD` at `150.5` is `150.5`
  yen, exactly halfway, so it rounds away from zero to `151 JPY`; at `151.5` it is `152 JPY`.
- `1.234 KWD` to USD at `3.25` is 4.0105 dollars, `4.01 USD`. `1 JPY` to USD at `0.0067` is 0.67 cents, `0.01 USD`.
- Negative amounts round symmetrically: `-1.00 USD` at `150.5` is `-151 JPY`.
- `1.00 USD` to EUR at `0.125` is 12.5 cents, which rounds to `0.13 EUR`.
- No rate: `CurrencyError` as for `rate`. An amount that is not a `Money`, or an unknown `dst`: `CurrencyError`.
- Converting back and forth is **not** exact and I do not expect it to be.

**`entries()`** returns every stored rate (not the inverses) as a list of `(src, dst, on, rate)` tuples, `rate` a
`Fraction`, sorted by `src`, then `dst`, then date. An empty table gives `[]`.

**`remove(src, dst, on)`** deletes the rate stored for exactly that source, destination and day and returns nothing.
It does not look at inverses: removing `EUR -> USD` when only `USD -> EUR` was set is an error. With no such entry,
`CurrencyError` with exactly the message `no rate USD -> EUR set on 2024-03-01` (the codes and day of the request).
Other dates are untouched: after removing the later of two USD -> EUR rates, lookups fall back to the earlier one.


### Periods

A **period** is a run of whole days, both ends included. `Period(start, end)` takes two dates (`.start`, `.end`). It
is immutable and hashable, and two periods with the same start and end are equal. An **empty** period is not allowed:
if `end` is before `start` the constructor raises `DateError` (its message names both dates). A one-day period
(`start == end`) is fine. A `start` or `end` that is not a `date` (a string, `None`) raises `DateError` too.

| member | meaning |
|---|---|
| `p.contains(d)` | `True` when `start <= d <= end` (both ends are inside); a non-date raises `DateError` |
| `p.days` | how many days it holds, both ends counted, as an `int`: January 2024 has `31` |
| `p.label` | the short name, below |
| `str(p)` | the same as the label |
| `p.next()` | the period that follows, below |

**Reading a period.** `Period.parse(text)` accepts exactly four shapes:

| text | period |
|---|---|
| `2024` | the whole year, 2024-01-01 to 2024-12-31 |
| `2024-03` | the month, 2024-03-01 to 2024-03-31 |
| `2024-Q1` | the quarter: Q1 is Jan-Mar, Q2 Apr-Jun, Q3 Jul-Sep, Q4 Oct-Dec |
| `2024-03-01..2024-03-31` | an explicit range of two full dates joined by two dots |

Everything else is a `DateError` whose message contains the whole text: `2024-3`, `2024-13`, `2024-Q0`, `2024-Q5`,
`2024-q1` (the Q is upper case), `2024Q1`, `24`, `12345`, `0000`, a lone date `2024-03-01` (write
`2024-03-01..2024-03-01`), `2024-03-01..`, `..2024-03-31`, `2024-03-01...2024-03-31`, `2024-03-01 .. 2024-03-31`,
`2024-03..2024-04`, `2024-02-30..2024-03-31`, an empty string, text with whitespace around it, and anything that is
not a string. A range ending before it starts (`2024-03-31..2024-03-01`) is an empty period, refused the same way;
`2024-03-05..2024-03-05` is fine.

**The label** names a period as briefly as possible, looking only at its dates, not at how it was written. Exactly one
whole calendar year is `2024`; a whole calendar month is `2024-03`; a whole calendar quarter is `2024-Q1`; anything
else is the range `2024-03-05..2024-03-20` (a single day is `2024-03-05..2024-03-05`). Years are four digits, so year
999 is `0999`. So `Period.parse("2024-01-01..2024-03-31").label` is `2024-Q1`, `Period.parse("2024-03-01..2024-03-31").label`
is `2024-03`, and `Period.parse("2024-04-01..2024-04-29").label` stays a range because April has 30 days.
`Period.parse(p.label) == p` for every period `p`.

**`p.next()`** is the following period of the same kind, the kind being decided by the dates alone, like the label:

- after a whole month, the next whole month (`2024-02` → `2024-03`, `2024-12` → `2025-01`; `2024-01` → `2024-02`, which
  has 29 days);
- after a whole quarter, the next quarter (`2024-Q4` → `2025-Q1`);
- after a whole year, the next year;
- after any other range, the range that starts the day after it ends and holds the same number of days:
  `2024-03-05..2024-03-14` → `2024-03-15..2024-03-24`, and a one-day period is followed by the next day.

A `next()` that would pass 9999-12-31 raises `DateError`.

   must be text without a line break (empty is fine), every tag must look like `salary`, `trip-2024` or `a_b` (ASCII

3. **Accounts.** Every posting's account must exist in the chart (message contains `unknown account` and the path;
   an invalid path is just unknown) and be usable on the transaction's date (see Accounts), otherwise the message
   contains the path and `is not open on` and the date. Posting to a parent account such as `Assets:Bank` is allowed. If
   the account was added with a currency, every amount posted to it must be in that currency, else the message contains
   `only holds` (for example `account Assets:Bank only holds USD, not EUR`).

   automatic conversion; `100.00 USD` out and `92.00 EUR` in does not balance (two currencies, each off), while 100 USD

### Exchange rates

A `RateTable` remembers what one currency was worth in another on particular days. A new table is empty.

```python
rates = RateTable()
rates.set("USD", "EUR", "0.9215", date(2024, 3, 1))
rates.rate("USD", "EUR", date(2024, 3, 15))   # Fraction(1843, 2000)
```

**`set(src, dst, rate_text, on)`** records that **one unit of `src` buys `rate_text` units of `dst`** from day `on` (a
`datetime.date`) onward. It returns nothing.

- `src` and `dst` must be currencies in the table and must differ; otherwise `CurrencyError`.
- `rate_text` must be **text** holding a positive decimal: digits, optionally a `.` followed by 1 to 8 digits. So
  `"150.5"`, `"0.9215"`, `"1"`, `"007.5"` and `"0.00000001"` are fine. Refused with `CurrencyError` (message containing
  the text): `"0"`, `"0.0"`, `"-1.5"`, `"+1.5"`, `".5"`, `"1."`, `"1,5"`, `"1e-3"`, `"1/2"`, `""`, `"abc"`, text with
  spaces or other kinds of digit characters, and anything with more than 8 decimals (`"1.123456789"`, even if the
  extra digits are zeros). Anything that is not text (a float, an int, a `Fraction`,
  `None`) is refused too: `0.9` and `2` are errors.
- `on` must be a `datetime.date`; a string like `"2024-03-01"`, `None` or a number is a `CurrencyError`, and so it is
  for `rate`, `convert` and `remove`. Every function here refuses an unknown or non-string currency code with
  `CurrencyError`.
- The rate is kept **exactly**, as a `fractions.Fraction`, never a float.
- Setting a rate for the same `(src, dst, on)` again **replaces** the earlier one.
- A rate is stored for one direction only; the opposite direction is worked out when asked.

A refused `set` changes nothing.

**`rate(src, dst, on)`** returns the rate in force on day `on` as a `Fraction`:

1. If `src == dst` it is `Fraction(1)` (both codes still have to be known currencies).
2. Otherwise, the rate set for `src -> dst` with the **latest date on or before `on`**. A rate dated the same day
   counts; a later one does not.
3. If no `src -> dst` rate is dated on or before `on`, the **inverse** of the rate set for `dst -> src` with the latest
   date on or before `on`, i.e. `1 / that_rate`, exactly.
4. Otherwise `CurrencyError` with the message `no rate USD -> EUR on 2024-03-01` (the codes and date asked for).

Two points I care about. A **direct rate always beats an inverse one**: as soon as any direct `src -> dst` rate is
dated on or before the day, it is used, even if an opposite-direction rate is more recent. And tallybook **never goes
through a third currency**: with `USD -> EUR` and `EUR -> GBP` set, `USD -> GBP` is an error. I would rather be told
than get a made-up rate.

After `set("USD", "EUR", "0.5", 2024-03-01)` and `set("USD", "EUR", "0.75", 2024-03-10)`:

| asked | answer |
|---|---|
| `rate("USD","EUR", 2024-02-29)` | error: no rate USD -> EUR on 2024-02-29 |
| `rate("USD","EUR", 2024-03-01)` | `Fraction(1, 2)` |
| `rate("USD","EUR", 2024-03-10)` | `Fraction(3, 4)` |
| `rate("EUR","USD", 2024-03-10)` | `Fraction(4, 3)` (the inverse of 3/4) |
| `rate("GBP","GBP", anything)` | `Fraction(1)` |

If `EUR -> USD` is also set to `"1.5"` on 2024-03-02, then `rate("EUR","USD", 2024-03-10)` is `3/2` (the direct rate
beats the inverse of `USD -> EUR`), while `rate("USD","EUR", ...)` still reads the `USD -> EUR` entries.

**`convert(money, dst, on)`** returns a `Money` in currency `dst`: the amount converted at `rate(money.currency, dst,
on)`. It converts the **value**, allowing for the different numbers of decimals, and rounds to a whole minor unit of
`dst` with `round_div` (see Money). With `e_src` and `e_dst` the two exponents, the new minor units are the old
minor units times the rate times `10 ** (e_dst - e_src)`, rounded.

- Converting to the same currency returns the same amount (no rate needed; `dst` must still be a known currency).
- `100.00 USD` to JPY at `150.5` is `15050 JPY` (10000 minor units × 150.5 ÷ 100). `1.00 USD` at `150.5` is `150.5`
  yen, exactly halfway, so it rounds away from zero to `151 JPY`; at `151.5` it is `152 JPY`.
- `1.234 KWD` to USD at `3.25` is 4.0105 dollars, `4.01 USD`. `1 JPY` to USD at `0.0067` is 0.67 cents, `0.01 USD`.
- Negative amounts round symmetrically: `-1.00 USD` at `150.5` is `-151 JPY`.
- `1.00 USD` to EUR at `0.125` is 12.5 cents, which rounds to `0.13 EUR`.
- No rate: `CurrencyError` as for `rate`. An amount that is not a `Money`, or an unknown `dst`: `CurrencyError`.
- Converting back and forth is **not** exact and I do not expect it to be.

**`entries()`** returns every stored rate (not the inverses) as a list of `(src, dst, on, rate)` tuples, `rate` a
`Fraction`, sorted by `src`, then `dst`, then date. An empty table gives `[]`.

**`remove(src, dst, on)`** deletes the rate stored for exactly that source, destination and day and returns nothing.
It does not look at inverses: removing `EUR -> USD` when only `USD -> EUR` was set is an error. With no such entry,
`CurrencyError` with exactly the message `no rate USD -> EUR set on 2024-03-01` (the codes and day of the request).
Other dates are untouched: after removing the later of two USD -> EUR rates, lookups fall back to the earlier one.


### Periods

A **period** is a run of whole days, both ends included. `Period(start, end)` takes two dates (`.start`, `.end`). It
is immutable and hashable, and two periods with the same start and end are equal. An **empty** period is not allowed:
if `end` is before `start` the constructor raises `DateError` (its message names both dates). A one-day period
(`start == end`) is fine. A `start` or `end` that is not a `date` (a string, `None`) raises `DateError` too.

| member | meaning |
|---|---|
| `p.contains(d)` | `True` when `start <= d <= end` (both ends are inside); a non-date raises `DateError` |
| `p.days` | how many days it holds, both ends counted, as an `int`: January 2024 has `31` |
| `p.label` | the short name, below |
| `str(p)` | the same as the label |
| `p.next()` | the period that follows, below |

**Reading a period.** `Period.parse(text)` accepts exactly four shapes:

| text | period |
|---|---|
| `2024` | the whole year, 2024-01-01 to 2024-12-31 |
| `2024-03` | the month, 2024-03-01 to 2024-03-31 |
| `2024-Q1` | the quarter: Q1 is Jan-Mar, Q2 Apr-Jun, Q3 Jul-Sep, Q4 Oct-Dec |
| `2024-03-01..2024-03-31` | an explicit range of two full dates joined by two dots |

Everything else is a `DateError` whose message contains the whole text: `2024-3`, `2024-13`, `2024-Q0`, `2024-Q5`,
`2024-q1` (the Q is upper case), `2024Q1`, `24`, `12345`, `0000`, a lone date `2024-03-01` (write
`2024-03-01..2024-03-01`), `2024-03-01..`, `..2024-03-31`, `2024-03-01...2024-03-31`, `2024-03-01 .. 2024-03-31`,
`2024-03..2024-04`, `2024-02-30..2024-03-31`, an empty string, text with whitespace around it, and anything that is
not a string. A range ending before it starts (`2024-03-31..2024-03-01`) is an empty period, refused the same way;
`2024-03-05..2024-03-05` is fine.

**The label** names a period as briefly as possible, looking only at its dates, not at how it was written. Exactly one
whole calendar year is `2024`; a whole calendar month is `2024-03`; a whole calendar quarter is `2024-Q1`; anything
else is the range `2024-03-05..2024-03-20` (a single day is `2024-03-05..2024-03-05`). Years are four digits, so year
999 is `0999`. So `Period.parse("2024-01-01..2024-03-31").label` is `2024-Q1`, `Period.parse("2024-03-01..2024-03-31").label`
is `2024-03`, and `Period.parse("2024-04-01..2024-04-29").label` stays a range because April has 30 days.
`Period.parse(p.label) == p` for every period `p`.

**`p.next()`** is the following period of the same kind, the kind being decided by the dates alone, like the label:

- after a whole month, the next whole month (`2024-02` → `2024-03`, `2024-12` → `2025-01`; `2024-01` → `2024-02`, which
  has 29 days);
- after a whole quarter, the next quarter (`2024-Q4` → `2025-Q1`);
- after a whole year, the next year;
- after any other range, the range that starts the day after it ends and holds the same number of days:
  `2024-03-05..2024-03-14` → `2024-03-15..2024-03-24`, and a one-day period is followed by the next day.

A `next()` that would pass 9999-12-31 raises `DateError`.

   and 92 EUR in two separate balanced pairs is fine. A transaction that does not balance is a `LedgerError` whose
   message contains `does not balance` and names every currency that is off with the sum of that currency's postings
   (for example `USD 5.00` or `JPY -300`), currencies in alphabetical order, separated by `, `.
5. **One amount may be left out.** If exactly one posting has `amount=None`, it gets whatever balances the transaction:
   the negative of the sum of the others. If the others are off in several currencies, that posting is replaced, in its
   place, by **one posting per currency that is off**, in alphabetical order of currency code, each with the same account
   and note. If the other postings already balance there is nothing to infer: `LedgerError`, message contains
   `nothing to infer`. Two or more postings without an amount: `LedgerError`, message contains
   `more than one posting without an amount`. The account-currency rule above applies to worked-out amounts too.
6. **Ids.** If `tx.id` is `None` the ledger assigns the next one: ids count 1, 2, 3, and **an id is never handed out
   again** in the same ledger, even after the transaction is removed (the next id is always one more than the highest id
   ever stored). I may give an id myself (my storage code does when it reloads a book): it must be an int of at least 1
   (not a `bool`) and not in use (message contains `already exists`), and later automatic ids continue after the highest.
7. Zero amounts are fine (`0.00 USD` postings are allowed).

### Budgets

A budget is `{"pattern": "Expenses:Food", "period_kind": "month", "amount": {money}, "start": "2024-01-01"}`.

- `GET /budgets` answers 200 with the budgets sorted by pattern, then period kind.
- `POST /budgets` with all four fields (the amount in either form) adds one and answers 201 with it; the budget module's checks apply. A second budget for the same pattern and period kind is a 409.
- `DELETE /budgets?pattern=Expenses:Food&period_kind=month` removes it and answers 200 with it; 404 if there is none.
- `GET /budgets/status?period=2024-03` (`period` required, read by `Period.parse`) answers 200 with the `BudgetLine.to_dict()` of each stored budget in force in that period (the others give no line), in the order `budget_status` returns them.

### Recurring items

A recurring item is `{"name": "rent", "schedule": "monthly on 1", "start": "2024-01-01", "end": null, "count": null, "template": {"payee": "Flat", "narration": "", "flag": "*", "tags": [], "postings": [{"account": ..., "amount": {money} or null, "note": ""}, ...]}}`. `schedule` is shown in its canonical text.

- `GET /recurring` answers 200 with the items sorted by name.
- `POST /recurring` with `name`, `schedule`, `start`, `template` (and optionally `end` and `count`) adds one and answers 201 with it. The template has `payee` and `postings` (required), `narration`, `flag`, `tags`, built like a transaction without a date (postings may leave out amounts; nothing is checked against the book until the item produces transactions). The recurring module's checks apply; an existing name is a 409.
- `DELETE /recurring?name=rent` removes the item (what it produced stays) and answers 200 with it; 404 if there is none.
- `POST /recurring/materialize` with `{"upto": "2024-06-30"}` (the field and the whole body are optional) runs `Store.materialize` and answers 200 `{"added": [transaction, ...]}` in the order the store made them. The horizon is `upto` and today, whichever is earlier (just today without `upto`), as the storage section says; a second run adds nothing (`{"added": []}`). If one is invalid, nothing is stored.

### Reports

`GET /reports/<name>` (`trial-balance`, `balance-sheet`, `income-statement`, `cashflow`, `register`) answers 200 with the report dict as the report section describes it, for the whole book. All take `format=json` (default) or `format=text` (`render_text` of the report as `text/plain; charset=utf-8`); any other format (and `format=` empty) is an error.

| report | parameters |
|---|---|
| `trial-balance` | `as_of` (a date; left out: all postings) |
| `balance-sheet` | `as_of` (a date; left out: all postings), `convert_to` (a currency code) |
| `income-statement` | `period` (required), `convert_to` |
| `cashflow` | `period` (required) |
| `register` | `account` (required), `period`, `rollup` (yes/no, default no) |

`period` is read by `Period.parse`. The rest is what the report functions do: a missing exchange rate or an unknown account in `register` is their `ReportError` or `CurrencyError` (validation), `balance-sheet` with `convert_to` but no `as_of` too. The server passes its `today` to `balance_sheet`, where it has no effect.

"""Helpers for the data command tests: run a command line, build books through the Store."""
import contextlib
import io
import os
import shutil
import tempfile
import unittest
from datetime import date

from tallybook.cli import main as cli_main
from tallybook.model import Posting, Transaction
from tallybook.money import Money
from tallybook.storage import Store


def _load_data_only():
    from tallybook.cli import data_commands  # noqa: F401


try:  # when the other command modules exist, run the real thing
    from tallybook.cli import book_commands, calc_commands  # noqa: F401
except ImportError:
    cli_main._load_commands = _load_data_only


def run(argv):
    """Run ``main(argv)``; returns (status, stdout, stderr)."""
    out, err = io.StringIO(), io.StringIO()
    with contextlib.redirect_stdout(out), contextlib.redirect_stderr(err):
        status = cli_main.main(list(argv))
    return status, out.getvalue(), err.getvalue()


def usd(text):
    return Money.of(text, "USD")


def tx(day, payee, *postings, **kw):
    posts = [Posting(a, None if m is None else usd(m)) for a, m in postings]
    return Transaction(date.fromisoformat(day), payee, kw.get("narration", ""), posts)


ACCOUNTS = ["Assets:Bank:Checking", "Assets:Cash", "Liabilities:Card", "Equity:Opening",
            "Income:Salary", "Expenses:Food", "Expenses:Rent"]

# the sample book of the reports section
SAMPLE = [
    ("2024-01-01", "Opening", ("Assets:Bank:Checking", "1000.00"), ("Equity:Opening", "-1000.00")),
    ("2024-03-01", "Acme", ("Assets:Bank:Checking", "2500.00"), ("Income:Salary", "-2500.00")),
    ("2024-03-02", "Market", ("Expenses:Food", "42.50"), ("Assets:Bank:Checking", "-42.50")),
    ("2024-03-05", "Landlord", ("Expenses:Rent", "900.00"), ("Liabilities:Card", "-900.00")),
    ("2024-03-10", "ATM", ("Assets:Cash", "100.00"), ("Assets:Bank:Checking", "-100.00")),
    ("2024-03-12", "Corner", ("Expenses:Food", "12.00"), ("Assets:Cash", "-12.00")),
    ("2024-04-02", "Card payoff", ("Liabilities:Card", "900.00"), ("Assets:Bank:Checking", "-900.00")),
    ("2024-04-03", "Market", ("Expenses:Food", "30.00"), ("Assets:Bank:Checking", "-30.00")),
]


class BookCase(unittest.TestCase):
    """A temporary directory per test; ``self.db`` is a new empty book; ``cli`` runs on it."""

    def setUp(self):
        self.dir = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="tb-cli-data-")
        self.addCleanup(shutil.rmtree, self.dir, True)
        self.db = os.path.join(self.dir, "book.db")
        with Store.open(self.db, create=True):
            pass

    def cli(self, *argv, today="2024-03-15"):
        pre = ["--db", self.db]
        if today is not None:
            pre += ["--today", today]
        return run(pre + list(argv))

    def store(self):
        return Store.open(self.db)

    def fill(self, accounts=ACCOUNTS, txs=SAMPLE):
        with Store.open(self.db) as s:
            for path in accounts:
                s.add_account(path)
            for item in txs:
                s.add_transaction(tx(item[0], item[1], *item[2:]))

    def ok(self, *argv, today="2024-03-15"):
        status, out, err = self.cli(*argv, today=today)
        self.assertEqual((status, err), (0, ""), "%r -> %r %r" % (argv, out, err))
        return out

    def fails(self, status, *argv, today="2024-03-15", contains=None):
        got, out, err = self.cli(*argv, today=today)
        self.assertEqual((got, out), (status, ""), "%r -> %r %r" % (argv, out, err))
        self.assertTrue(err.startswith("tallybook: "), err)
        self.assertTrue(err.endswith("\n"))
        if status == 2:
            self.assertEqual(err.splitlines()[-1], "Try 'tallybook --help'.")
            self.assertEqual(len(err.splitlines()), 2)
        else:
            self.assertEqual(len(err.splitlines()), 1)
        self.assertNotIn("Traceback", err)
        if contains is not None:
            self.assertIn(contains, err)
        return err

class BookCase(unittest.TestCase):
    """A temporary directory per test; ``self.db`` is a new empty book; ``cli`` runs on it."""

    def setUp(self):
        self.dir = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="tb-cli-data-")
        self.addCleanup(shutil.rmtree, self.dir, True)
        self.db = os.path.join(self.dir, "book.db")
        with Store.open(self.db, create=True):
            pass

    def cli(self, *argv, today="2024-03-15"):
        pre = ["--db", self.db]
        if today is not None:
            pre += ["--today", today]
        return run(pre + list(argv))

    def store(self):
        return Store.open(self.db)

    def fill(self, accounts=ACCOUNTS, txs=SAMPLE):
        with Store.open(self.db) as s:
            for path in accounts:
                s.add_account(path)
            for item in txs:
                s.add_transaction(tx(item[0], item[1], *item[2:]))

    def ok(self, *argv, today="2024-03-15"):
        status, out, err = self.cli(*argv, today=today)
        self.assertEqual((status, err), (0, ""), "%r -> %r %r" % (argv, out, err))
        return out

    def fails(self, status, *argv, today="2024-03-15", contains=None):
        got, out, err = self.cli(*argv, today=today)
        self.assertEqual((got, out), (status, ""), "%r -> %r %r" % (argv, out, err))
        self.assertTrue(err.startswith("tallybook: "), err)
        self.assertTrue(err.endswith("\n"))
        if status == 2:
            self.assertEqual(err.splitlines()[-1], "Try 'tallybook --help'.")
            self.assertEqual(len(err.splitlines()), 2)
        else:
            self.assertEqual(len(err.splitlines()), 1)
        self.assertNotIn("Traceback", err)
        if contains is not None:
            self.assertIn(contains, err)
        return err

            (["rate", "set", "GBP", "USD", "1.27", "--on=2024-02-01"],

             "USD   EUR  2024-01-05      0.9\n"

        self.assertEqual(self.store().rate_rows(),

                         "created 5 transactions\n")
        self.assertEqual(self.ok("recurring", "materialize", "--upto", "2024-06-15", today="2024-05-10"),
                         "created 0 transactions\n")
        self.assertEqual(
            self.ok("recurring", "list"),
            "Name  Schedule                       Start       End         Count  Through     Payee\n"
            "----  -----------------------------  ----------  ----------  -----  ----------  -----\n"

        data = json.loads(out)
        self.assertEqual([(t["id"], t["date"], t["payee"]) for t in data],
                         [(14, "2024-05-15", "Gym"), (15, "2024-05-29", "Gym"), (16, "2024-06-01", "Flat")]

        # gym has made its 5 dates (04-03, 04-17, 05-01, 05-15, 05-29); rent adds June 1

class RobustnessTests(BookCase):
    def test_huge_numbers(self):
        digits = "1" * 5000
        cases = [
            ["rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", digits],
            ["rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", digits + ".12345678", "--on", "2024-01-01"],
            ["budget", "add", "Expenses:Food", digits + ".00 USD"],
            ["recurring", "add", "big", "daily", "P", "-p", "Assets:Cash %s.00 USD" % digits,
             "-p", "Assets:Bank:Checking -%s.00 USD" % digits],
        ]
        for argv in cases:
            with self.subTest(argv=argv[:3]):
                self.assertEqual(self.cli(*argv)[0], 0)
        out = self.ok("rate", "list")
        self.assertIn(digits + ".12345678", out)
        self.assertEqual(self.store().rate_rows()[0][3], digits)
        self.assertIn(digits + ".00 USD", self.ok("budget", "list"))
        data = json.loads(self.ok("recurring", "list", "--json"))
        self.assertEqual(data[0]["template"]["postings"][1]["amount"]["amount"], "-%s.00" % digits)
        self.assertEqual(self.ok("recurring", "remove", "big"), "removed recurring big\n")
        self.assertEqual(self.ok("budget", "remove", "Expenses:Food"), "removed budget Expenses:Food per month\n")

    def test_huge_numbers_are_never_a_crash(self):
        digits = "9" * 5000
        for argv in (["recurring", "add", "x", "daily", "P", "--count", digits],
                     ["budget", "add", "Expenses:Food", digits + " USD", "--per", "week"],
                     ["rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", "0." + digits]):
            with self.subTest(argv=argv[:3]):
                self.fails(1, *argv)

    def test_largest_count(self):
        self.assertEqual(self.ok("recurring", "add", "x", "daily", "P", "--count", "9" * 18), "added recurring x\n")
        self.assertEqual(json.loads(self.ok("recurring", "list", "--json"))[0]["count"], 10 ** 18 - 1)

    def test_non_ascii_text(self):
        self.assertEqual(self.ok("recurring", "add", "caf", "daily", "Café ☕", "--narration", "über",
                                 "-p", "Assets:Cash 1.00 USD ; été", "-p", "Assets:Bank:Checking"),
                         "added recurring caf\n")
        out = self.ok("recurring", "list")
        self.assertTrue(out.splitlines()[2].endswith("Café ☕"))
        data = json.loads(self.ok("recurring", "list", "--json"))
        self.assertEqual(data[0]["template"]["postings"][0]["note"], "été")
        self.assertEqual(data[0]["template"]["narration"], "über")
        self.fails(1, "recurring", "add", "x", "daily", "P", "--tag", "café")

    def test_failures_leave_stdout_empty_and_the_book_alone(self):
        self.fill()
        before = self.store().info()
        for argv in (["rate", "set", "USD", "USD", "1"], ["budget", "add", "Expenses:Food", "0 USD"],
                     ["recurring", "add", "x", "nonsense", "P"], ["report", "register", "Nope"]):
            with self.subTest(argv=argv):
                self.fails(1, *argv)
        self.assertEqual(self.store().info(), before)

    def test_closing_pipe_text_ends_with_one_newline(self):
        self.fill()
        for argv in (["report", "balance-sheet"], ["budget", "status"], ["rate", "list"]):
            out = self.ok(*argv)
            if out:
                self.assertTrue(out.endswith("\n") and not out.endswith("\n\n"))
                self.assertFalse(any(line != line.rstrip(" ") for line in out.splitlines()))

    def test_materialize(self):
        self.fill()
        self.ok(*self.RENT)
        self.ok(*self.GYM)
        # the horizon is the earlier of --upto and today
        self.assertEqual(self.ok("recurring", "materialize", "--upto", "2024-06-15", today="2024-05-10"),
                         "created 5 transactions\n")
        self.assertEqual(self.ok("recurring", "materialize", "--upto", "2024-06-15", today="2024-05-10"),
                         "created 0 transactions\n")
        self.assertEqual(
            self.ok("recurring", "list"),
            "Name  Schedule                       Start       End         Count  Through     Payee\n"
            "----  -----------------------------  ----------  ----------  -----  ----------  -----\n"
            "gym   every 2 weeks from 2024-04-03  2024-04-03  2024-12-31  5      2024-05-10  Gym\n"

        out = self.ok("recurring", "materialize", "--upto", "2024-06-15", "--json", today="2024-06-30")
        data = json.loads(out)
        self.assertEqual([(t["id"], t["date"], t["payee"]) for t in data],
                         [(14, "2024-05-15", "Gym"), (15, "2024-05-29", "Gym"), (16, "2024-06-01", "Flat")]

        # gym has made its 5 dates (04-03, 04-17, 05-01, 05-15, 05-29); rent adds June 1

class RateTests(BookCase):
    def test_set_list_remove(self):
        steps = [
            (["rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", "0.92", "--on", "2024-03-01"],
             "set 1 USD = 0.92 EUR on 2024-03-01\n"),
            (["rate", "set", "GBP", "USD", "1.27", "--on=2024-02-01"],
             "set 1 GBP = 1.27 USD on 2024-02-01\n"),
            (["rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", "0.9", "--on", "2024-01-05"],
             "set 1 USD = 0.9 EUR on 2024-01-05\n"),
            (["rate", "set", "USD", "JPY", "0150.50"], "set 1 USD = 0150.50 JPY on 2024-03-15\n"),
            (["rate", "list"],
             "From  To   Date        Rate\n"
             "----  ---  ----------  -------\n"
             "GBP   USD  2024-02-01     1.27\n"
             "USD   EUR  2024-01-05      0.9\n"
             "USD   EUR  2024-03-01     0.92\n"
             "USD   JPY  2024-03-15  0150.50\n"),
            (["rate", "remove", "USD", "EUR", "--on", "2024-01-05"],
             "removed rate USD -> EUR on 2024-01-05\n"),
            (["rate", "remove", "USD", "JPY"], "removed rate USD -> JPY on 2024-03-15\n"),
            (["rate", "list"],
             "From  To   Date        Rate\n"
             "----  ---  ----------  ----\n"
             "GBP   USD  2024-02-01  1.27\n"
             "USD   EUR  2024-03-01  0.92\n"),
        ]
        for argv, expected in steps:
            with self.subTest(argv=argv):
                self.assertEqual(self.ok(*argv), expected)

    def test_set_replaces_same_day(self):
        self.ok("rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", "0.9", "--on", "2024-03-01")
        self.ok("rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", "0.95", "--on", "2024-03-01")
        self.assertEqual(self.store().rate_rows(),
                         [("USD", "EUR", date(2024, 3, 1), "0.95")])

    def test_list_json_and_empty(self):
        self.assertEqual(self.ok("rate", "list"), "")
        self.assertEqual(self.ok("rate", "list", "--json"), "[]\n")
        self.ok("rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", "0.92", "--on", "2024-03-01")
        self.assertEqual(self.ok("rate", "list", "--json"),
                         '[\n  {\n    "date": "2024-03-01",\n    "from": "USD",\n'
                         '    "rate": "0.92",\n    "to": "EUR"\n  }\n]\n')

    def test_today_default_comes_from_the_global_option(self):
        out = self.ok("rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", "2", today="2030-12-31")
        self.assertEqual(out, "set 1 USD = 2 EUR on 2030-12-31\n")
        self.assertEqual(self.ok("rate", "remove", "USD", "EUR", today="2030-12-31"),
                         "removed rate USD -> EUR on 2030-12-31\n")

    def test_refusals(self):
        self.ok("rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", "0.92", "--on", "2024-03-01")
        cases = [
            (["rate", "set", "USD", "USD", "1"], "itself"),
            (["rate", "set", "USD", "XXX", "1"], "XXX"),
            (["rate", "set", "usd", "EUR", "1"], "usd"),
            (["rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", "0"], "'0'"),
            (["rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", "-1"], "-1"),
            (["rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", "+1"], "+1"),
            (["rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", "1e3"], "1e3"),
            (["rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", ".5"], ".5"),
            (["rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", "1.123456789"], "1.123456789"),
            (["rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", ""], "invalid rate"),
            (["rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", "1", "--on", "2024-02-30"], "2024-02-30"),
            (["rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", "1", "--on", "2024-2-3"], "2024-2-3"),
            (["rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", "1", "--on", ""], "invalid date"),
            (["rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", "1", "--on="], "invalid date"),
            (["rate", "remove", "USD", "EUR", "--on", "2024-03-02"], "no rate USD -> EUR set on 2024-03-02"),
            (["rate", "remove", "EUR", "USD", "--on", "2024-03-01"], "no rate EUR -> USD set on 2024-03-01"),
            (["rate", "remove", "USD", "EUR", "--on", "nope"], "nope"),

            with self.subTest(argv=argv):
                self.fails(1, *argv, contains=text)

    def test_values_that_look_like_options(self):
        # "--" ends the options; the value after it is plain even with a leading dash
        self.fails(1, "rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", "--", "-1", contains="-1")
        self.assertEqual(self.ok("rate", "set", "--", "USD", "EUR", "1.5", "--on", "2024-01-01")
                         if False else self.ok("rate", "set", "--on", "2024-01-01", "--", "USD", "EUR", "1.5"),
                         "set 1 USD = 1.5 EUR on 2024-01-01\n")
        self.fails(1, "rate", "remove", "USD", "EUR", "--on", "-5", contains="-5")

class RobustnessTests(BookCase):
    def test_huge_numbers(self):
        digits = "1" * 5000
        cases = [
            ["rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", digits],
            ["rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", digits + ".12345678", "--on", "2024-01-01"],
            ["budget", "add", "Expenses:Food", digits + ".00 USD"],
            ["recurring", "add", "big", "daily", "P", "-p", "Assets:Cash %s.00 USD" % digits,
             "-p", "Assets:Bank:Checking -%s.00 USD" % digits],
        ]
        for argv in cases:
            with self.subTest(argv=argv[:3]):
                self.assertEqual(self.cli(*argv)[0], 0)
        out = self.ok("rate", "list")
        self.assertIn(digits + ".12345678", out)
        self.assertEqual(self.store().rate_rows()[0][3], digits)
        self.assertIn(digits + ".00 USD", self.ok("budget", "list"))
        data = json.loads(self.ok("recurring", "list", "--json"))
        self.assertEqual(data[0]["template"]["postings"][1]["amount"]["amount"], "-%s.00" % digits)
        self.assertEqual(self.ok("recurring", "remove", "big"), "removed recurring big\n")
        self.assertEqual(self.ok("budget", "remove", "Expenses:Food"), "removed budget Expenses:Food per month\n")

    def test_huge_numbers_are_never_a_crash(self):
        digits = "9" * 5000
        for argv in (["recurring", "add", "x", "daily", "P", "--count", digits],
                     ["budget", "add", "Expenses:Food", digits + " USD", "--per", "week"],
                     ["rate", "set", "USD", "EUR", "0." + digits]):
            with self.subTest(argv=argv[:3]):
                self.fails(1, *argv)

    def test_largest_count(self):
        self.assertEqual(self.ok("recurring", "add", "x", "daily", "P", "--count", "9" * 18), "added recurring x\n")
        self.assertEqual(json.loads(self.ok("recurring", "list", "--json"))[0]["count"], 10 ** 18 - 1)

    def test_non_ascii_text(self):
        self.assertEqual(self.ok("recurring", "add", "caf", "daily", "Café ☕", "--narration", "über",
                                 "-p", "Assets:Cash 1.00 USD ; été", "-p", "Assets:Bank:Checking"),
                         "added recurring caf\n")
        out = self.ok("recurring", "list")
        self.assertTrue(out.splitlines()[2].endswith("Café ☕"))
        data = json.loads(self.ok("recurring", "list", "--json"))
        self.assertEqual(data[0]["template"]["postings"][0]["note"], "été")
        self.assertEqual(data[0]["template"]["narration"], "über")
        self.fails(1, "recurring", "add", "x", "daily", "P", "--tag", "café")

    def test_failures_leave_stdout_empty_and_the_book_alone(self):
        self.fill()
        before = self.store().info()
        for argv in (["rate", "set", "USD", "USD", "1"], ["budget", "add", "Expenses:Food", "0 USD"],
                     ["recurring", "add", "x", "nonsense", "P"], ["report", "register", "Nope"]):
            with self.subTest(argv=argv):
                self.fails(1, *argv)
        self.assertEqual(self.store().info(), before)

    def test_closing_pipe_text_ends_with_one_newline(self):
        self.fill()
        for argv in (["report", "balance-sheet"], ["budget", "status"], ["rate", "list"]):

Files written: `tallybook/cli/data_commands.py` (all 12 commands plus `parse_posting_arg`), `tests/test_cli_data.py` and `tests/helpers_cli_data.py`.

- **Tests:** 45 tests pass on Python 3.13 and 3.9.25. All three command modules exist now, so the helper's `_load_commands` patch is skipped and these runs went through the unmodified loader.
- **Core defects / requested changes:** none to `core.py`, `main.py` or `render.py`. One thing to know: `parse_args` matches shorts against the literal token, so `Opt(..., short="-p")` needs the dash. `short="p"` fails with "unexpected argument: -p". `book_commands.py` already uses `"-p"`.
- **Decisions:**
  - `recurring materialize` passes both `upto` and `today=ctx.today`. The horizon is therefore the earlier of the two, which matches the storage and API sections.
  - `recurring add` rejects a bad flag, a bad tag, or a line break in payee, narration or posting note with exit 1. The spec says nothing about this, but otherwise `materialize` would fail on every later run.
  - Arguments are parsed (dates, periods, counts, postings) before the book is opened. A bad value therefore wins over a missing book.
  - A table with no rows prints nothing, and `--json` prints `[]`.
  - Any `ValueError` or `OverflowError` that escapes a handler becomes exit 1 `invalid number: ...`. 5000-digit rates and amounts succeed, because `tallybook/__init__` already disables Python's int-digit limit.
